clinicalPearls: A disorder of gut-brain interaction defined by recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and associated with a change in stool frequency or form
It is subclassified by predominant bowel habit into constipation-predominant, diarrhoea-predominant, mixed and unclassified types
It is a positive clinical diagnosis based on symptom criteria with limited targeted testing, not merely a diagnosis of exclusion
Alarm features such as weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, older age of onset or a family history of bowel cancer warrant investigation
Coeliac serology and, where indicated, faecal calprotectin help exclude coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease
Management combines dietary measures, symptom-directed pharmacotherapy and psychological therapies
reference.pathophysiology: Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which altered gastrointestinal motility, visceral hypersensitivity, changes in the gut microbiota, low-grade mucosal immune activation, and disturbed central processing of visceral signals combine to produce pain and altered bowel habit. Bidirectional signalling along the gut-brain axis, often modulated by stress and psychological factors, amplifies visceral perception. There is no structural or biochemical abnormality that defines the condition, which is characterised instead by its symptom pattern.
additionalInvestigations: Faecal calprotectin where inflammatory bowel disease is a concern
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Colonoscopy or further imaging when alarm features are present
redFlags: New symptoms in an older patient
Family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and relapsing but benign, and most patients achieve worthwhile symptom control with an individualised combination of diet, medication and psychological approaches.
pitfalls: Treating it purely as a diagnosis of exclusion and over-investigating
Missing coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease presenting similarly
Overlooking the role of psychological factors and the gut-brain axis in management
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
